item.title: Anthropic IPO: SpaceX stands to make out big from AI lab's compute spending
item.author: Pras Subramanian
item.description:
Anthropic IPO: SpaceX stands to make out big from AI lab's compute spending
2026-10-27
Por Pras Subramanian
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/anthropic-ipo-spacex-stands-to-make-out-big-from-ai-labs-compute-spending-184620862.html
One company that's going to benefit big time from Anthropic's (ANTH.PVT) growth over the coming years: SpaceX (SPCX).
In its IPO prospectus filed on Monday, Anthropic outlined how much it could spend with SpaceX over the coming years after entering into several agreements with SpaceXAI to access its NVIDIA (NVDA) GPUs for compute.
"Under the SpaceXAI Arrangements, we agreed to spend an aggregate of up to $120.5 billion over terms extending into 2029, consisting of approximately $3.1 billion in the aggregate per month once all capacity has been delivered, which we expect in December 2026, with different fees during capacity ramping periods," the company said.
While it was known that SpaceX and Anthropic had contracted for a billion dollar+ per month compute deal, it was not known how long the deal would last or the possible total outlay. A 90-day advance notice for cancellation was also disclosed.
For SpaceX, it's another feather in its hat for its AI data center compute business, which is now shown to be durable. SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen discussed growth in the company's SI business ventures during its Q3 earnings call.
"There are many customers asking for compute, and we're actively building the supply to meet both internal and external demand. We expect to have additional new customers in future deals and will continuously evaluate the highest-margin usage for our compute assets across both new and existing cloud service agreements, including serving inference for our own SI products. What we're seeing in the market is extraordinary."
Johnsen added that at current pricing, new compute deployments are generating a payback of less than a year, with pricing "currently tracking slightly above the high end of the 30 to $50 per watt range." Johnsen had previously said he expects SpaceX to hit an annual recurring revenue figure (ARR) of $100 billion by year-end.
Not to be outdone, CEO Elon Musk said he sees SpaceX's ARR hitting between $500 billion and $1 trillion by the end of 2027. Musk is spending heavily too, with SpaceX confirming a new $40 billion deal for Nvidia chips, leased from Apollo Global. (Disclosure: Yahoo is a portfolio company of funds managed by affiliates of Apollo Global Management.)
Musk also sees SpaceX as a competitor with a substantial advantage over smaller "neocloud" providers, owing to its credit rating and ancillary revenue streams such as Starlink and launches. The SpaceX CEO sees debt markets all but closed to the smaller AI data center players.

item.title: Anthropic publicly files IPO prospectus, noting strong revenue growth and massive spending
item.author: Daniel Howley
item.description:
Anthropic publicly files IPO prospectus, noting strong revenue growth and massive spending
2026-10-27
Por Daniel Howley
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/anthropic-publicly-files-ipo-prospectus-noting-strong-revenue-growth-and-massive-spending-131807138.html
Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) has publicly filed its S-1 investment prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission, giving investors a look at the company's most important financial information ahead of its initial public offering.
The company, which will trade under the ticker symbol ANT, said it generated $16.3 billion in revenue in the six-month period that ended in June, more than the $4.6 billion the company saw in all of 2025.
But the company also spent $9 billion on AI infrastructure in the first six months of the year, ahead of the $7.3 billion it spent throughout 2025.
Roughly one-fifth of Anthropic's revenue came from two customers. The remainder came from a small handful of clients.
According to the S-1, Anthropic saw a net loss of $80.7 billion through June, though the vast majority of that was the result of accounting charges.
The company lost $42 billion in 2025.
The AI giant also plans to spend upward of $430 billion on locked-in cloud computing deals with companies including Amazon and Google, major Anthropic investors, and others in the years ahead. Toss in cancellable and smaller deals, the total reaches as much as $637 billion.
The company's market debut will test investors' appetite for a second public listing by a firm with an already massive valuation. SpaceX (SPCX) went public on June 12 at $150 per share and ended the day 20% higher.
Helmed by CEO Dario Amodei, who co-founded the company with his sister Daniela, the company's president, Anthropic established a strong foothold in the enterprise market with its Claude chatbot, the popular AI coding tool Claude Code, and Claude Cowork.
But the S-1 also reveals Anthropic's fears that models may develop capabilities the company doesn't anticipate.
The filing lays out a host of potentially damaging scenarios in which its AI models could cause real-world harm. Anthropic said that could limit the company's ability to cover any potential damages.
In an early September essay, Amodei called on the AI industry to slow the development of frontier AI models over fears that they could become too powerful for humans to control. The piece, coupled with statements by former and current researchers at AI companies, sent shockwaves through the industry and raised concerns that the technology could "kill all humans."
Experts dispute those claims, saying that the risks surrounding AI stem from basic cybersecurity protections and from preventing people and governments from using it for things like identity theft, discrimination, and labor displacement.

item.title: Oil settles lower on peace hopes, Saudi attacks limit losses
item.author: Siddharth Cavale
item.description:
Oil settles lower on peace hopes, Saudi attacks limit losses
2026-10-27
Por Siddharth Cavale
https://finance.yahoo.com/news/oil-prices-down-almost-1-232445179.html
By Siddharth Cavale
NEW YORK, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Brent crude futures finished lower on Monday amid hopes of easing hostilities in the Middle East, but persistent attacks on key producer Saudi Arabia and maritime shipping kept investors wary and prices hovering near six-month highs.
Brent finished the day down 91 cents, or 0.8%, at $115.81 a barrel while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures closed down $1.51, or 1.46%, at $101.76 a barrel.
Both benchmarks retreated after strong gains on Friday, when Brent settled more than $3 higher to post a weekly gain of 6%, while WTI rose 2.3% for the week.
Investor focus remained on tensions in the Middle East after Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they struck pumping stations on Saudi Arabia's East-West crude oil pipeline and Riyadh airport over the weekend. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the Houthi attacks.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, however, said on Monday it had destroyed three drones targeting Riyadh and the kingdom's southern regions.
Hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough in the Middle East conflict, which began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran and later spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen, weighed on oil prices earlier in the session, with Brent falling more than $2 a barrel.
Qatari mediators travelled to Tehran on Sunday in coordination with the United States to seek ways to ease regional tensions, according to an official briefed on the matter.
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistanheld talks with Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday as part of efforts to prevent further escalation in the region.
The talks were the first high-level contact between Iran and the three nations, which signed a mutual defence pact in August.
At the conclusion, the four countries agreed to continue talks with a view to strengthening cooperation in peace and security, Iranian state media reported.
Egypt's parliament authorized President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia defend itself, raising the prospect of Egyptian military support for the kingdom.
WORST MONTH FOR MARITIME ATTACKS
The effects of the US-Israeli war with Iran that began on February 28 continue to reverberate as companies adjust to the disruptions of commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb Strait caused by the conflict.
October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, a think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017.

item.title: Microsoft offers voluntary buyout to 60,000 employees
item.author: Grace O'Donnell
item.description:
Microsoft offers voluntary buyout to 60,000 employees
2026-10-27
Por Grace O'Donnell
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/microsoft-offers-voluntary-buyout-to-60000-employees-160011034.html
Microsoft (MSFT) announced on Monday that it was offering voluntary buyouts to roughly 60,000 employees as it looks to reshape its organization for the AI era.
"The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter," Amy Coleman, Microsoft's executive vice president and chief people officer, wrote in a memo to employees.
The company is reportedly offering buyouts to employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom, and the United States at level 70 and below, which includes some senior-level personnel.
The announcement follows Microsoft's first voluntary retirement program, which it announced in May. The retirement packages offered ranged from eight to 39 weeks of base pay, depending on employees' positions and tenure.
The offers to staff come as Microsoft plans to spend $190 billion on capital expenditures in 2026, largely tied to its investments in artificial intelligence.
All eyes will be on the Big Tech giant on Wednesday, when Microsoft releases its quarterly earnings and provides an update on its capex plans and Azure cloud growth.

item.title: CoreWeave, AI landlord stocks sink to lowest levels in more than a year as the price of insuring CoreWeave's debt doubles
item.author: Jared Blikre
item.description:
CoreWeave, AI landlord stocks sink to lowest levels in more than a year as the price of insuring CoreWeave's debt doubles
2026-10-27
Por Jared Blikre
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/coreweave-ai-landlord-stocks-sink-to-lowest-levels-in-more-than-a-year-as-the-price-of-insuring-coreweaves-debt-doubles-140909005.html
CoreWeave, AI landlord stocks sink to lowest levels in more than a year as the price of insuring CoreWeave's debt doubles
Wall Street is still paying up for the companies that buy AI computing power. It's dumping the ones that borrowed billions to rent it out.
Think of the neoclouds as AI's landlords. They take on heavy debt to buy Nvidia (NVDA) chips, then rent out the computing power to companies building AI. That works fine while money is cheap and tenants keep signing leases. It gets dicey when lenders start asking questions.
They're asking now. A Yahoo Finance basket of eight neoclouds has lost more than 40% since late July. Microsoft (MSFT), one of the biggest renters of AI computing power, has gained nearly as much.
CoreWeave (CRWV), the biggest of the group, closed Friday at its lowest since May 2025, then slid to about $51 early Monday before buyers stepped in. IREN (IREN), Core Scientific (CORZ), and Cipher Mining (CIFR) closed Friday at their lowest in more than a year, and Galaxy Digital (GLXY) hit a record low for its US listing.
The bond market is sending the same message
Investors can buy insurance against a company defaulting on its debt, called a credit default swap. For CoreWeave, that insurance now costs more than twice as much as it did in early June, according to Bloomberg data.
At today's price, the market is effectively betting on better-than-even odds that CoreWeave defaults within five years, by Yahoo Finance calculations. That's double the odds of a year ago. It's a price with plenty of fear baked in, not a forecast.
Last week, CoreWeave flirted with a bear trap — a dip that snaps back and burns traders betting on more losses. The bounce didn't stick, and the cost of insuring its debt kept climbing.

2026-10-27

Por Jared Blikre

https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/coreweave-ai-landlord-stocks-sink-to-lowest-levels-in-more-than-a-year-as-the-price-of-insuring-coreweaves-debt-doubles-140909005.html

CoreWeave, AI landlord stocks sink to lowest levels in more than a year as the price of insuring CoreWeave's debt doubles

Wall Street is still paying up for the companies that buy AI computing power. It's dumping the ones that borrowed billions to rent it out.

Think of the neoclouds as AI's landlords. They take on heavy debt to buy Nvidia (NVDA) chips, then rent out the computing power to companies building AI. That works fine while money is cheap and tenants keep signing leases. It gets dicey when lenders start asking questions.

They're asking now. A Yahoo Finance basket of eight neoclouds has lost more than 40% since late July. Microsoft (MSFT), one of the biggest renters of AI computing power, has gained nearly as much.

CoreWeave (CRWV), the biggest of the group, closed Friday at its lowest since May 2025, then slid to about $51 early Monday before buyers stepped in. IREN (IREN), Core Scientific (CORZ), and Cipher Mining (CIFR) closed Friday at their lowest in more than a year, and Galaxy Digital (GLXY) hit a record low for its US listing.

The bond market is sending the same message

Investors can buy insurance against a company defaulting on its debt, called a credit default swap. For CoreWeave, that insurance now costs more than twice as much as it did in early June, according to Bloomberg data.

At today's price, the market is effectively betting on better-than-even odds that CoreWeave defaults within five years, by Yahoo Finance calculations. That's double the odds of a year ago. It's a price with plenty of fear baked in, not a forecast.

item.title: BofA’s Hartnett Sees Risk-Off Mood Lasting Until Mid-November
item.author: Levin Stamm
item.description:
BofA’s Hartnett Sees Risk-Off Mood Lasting Until Mid-November
2026-10-26
Por Levin Stamm
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/bofa-hartnett-sees-risk-off-094854981.html
(Bloomberg) -- Investors' risk-off mood is likely to continue well into November, according to Bank of America Corp.'s Michael Hartnett, in another sign of how jitters around the artificial intelligence trade and the US midterm elections have held back equity markets.
Most Read from Bloomberg
"We stay tactically risk-off until mid-Nov," the strategist wrote in a note to clients Friday. "Expect down-in-yields, down-in-stocks, down-in US dollar trade."
Hartnett said the market still needs to fully price a Democratic victory in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, which would be negative for earnings growth as it would result in an end to the current low-tax, low-regulation regime.
Another factor that would signal a revival of risk appetites would be the European Central Bank or French government stepping in to reverse the rout in French bond yields, Hartnett said. A peak in AI hyperscaler debt spreads, which have spooked markets recently, could also be brought about by cuts to capital spending or an "extreme equity issuance announcement," he said.
Investors are continuing to pile into the AI-related sectors. EPFR Global data cited by the bank showed the largest weekly inflows into technology stocks since July. A Bank of America survey this month also showed that global investors are the most exposed to tech since August 2020.
In recent days, though, they've also taken a defensive turn, looking for shelter from a series of risks ranging from climbing oil prices and higher borrowing costs as well as worries that the AI trade is starting to exhibit bubble-like conditions.
Billionaire Ken Griffin warned this week that investors are "almost certainly" in the midst of an AI bubble. An equal-weighted version of the S&P 500 Index — a proxy for market breadth — on Thursday had its best day since 2024 relative to the market-cap weighted S&P 500. Defensive consumer staple stocks, meanwhile, are on track for their best month since 1998.
Most Read from Bloomberg Businessweek
2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: US Business Activity Expands, Prices Surge by Most Since 2022
item.author: Jeffrey Sparshott
item.description:
US Business Activity Expands, Prices Surge by Most Since 2022
2026-10-26
Por Jeffrey Sparshott
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/us-business-activity-expands-prices-134500339.html
(Bloomberg) -- US business activity grew at a slightly slower pace in October but remained close to a multi-year high as robust demand pushed new orders, employment and prices higher.
Most Read from Bloomberg
The S&P Global flash composite index fell 0.8 point to 57.6 in October, data released Friday showed. That was the second-highest reading since 2022. Figures above 50 indicate expansion.
A gauge of selling prices rose at the fastest pace in more than four years, reflecting a sharp rise in the cost of energy, transportation and raw materials.
"Cost pressures remain a key concern, notably as the renewed surge in oil prices reverberates through to impact a wide variety of goods and services," Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said in a statement.
Bottlenecks are also getting worse. Supplier delivery times lengthened the most since 2022, with S&P Global citing material and labor shortages as well as overloaded suppliers and shipping delays.
Even so, Williamson said that, outside the pandemic reopening, US businesses are enjoying their strongest period of growth since 2015.
Strong consumer spending, AI-fueled investment and defense outlays have all bolstered US businesses this year. New orders, a gauge of demand, posted the fastest growth in four-and-a-half years in October.
Firms are responding by adding more workers. The composite index for employment was the second-highest in four years, and the manufacturing index showed factory headcount advancing at the fastest pace since 2012.
Looking ahead, investment in artificial intelligence and related technologies is anticipated to support demand and the broader economy next year, too. Forecasters raised their estimates for private investment growth in the third quarter and across all of 2027 in the latest Bloomberg News survey of economists.
The group's overall manufacturing index inched up to 56, the strongest since May 2022, while a gauge of activity at service providers eased.
--With assistance from Julia Fanzeres, Dana Morgan and Aidan Williams.
Most Read from Bloomberg Businessweek
2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: 'A cyclical downturn is inevitable' in an AI crash: Strategist Dario Perkins
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
'A cyclical downturn is inevitable' in an AI crash: Strategist Dario Perkins
2026-10-26
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/a-cyclical-downturn-is-inevitable-in-an-ai-crash-strategist-dario-perkins-170539090.html
If the weakness in tech stocks continues to gain steam, it could end up being really ugly for investors, given how aggressively they have gone into tech stocks in recent years.
That's the warning in a new paper making the rounds on Friday from TS Lombard strategist Dario Perkins titled "Wargaming the AI Crash."
"The reality, of course, is that it is hard to identify the exact trigger for an AI crash. But we can model the fallout. In terms of financial markets, the impact is likely to be sizable. US stocks would be hit hard, with (at least) a 30% decline. That would wipe out around $20 trillion in market cap," Perkins said. Across debt markets and private credits, he estimated "$125–200 billion in losses. Spreads would blow out, and we should expect a wave of tech-related defaults."
"The weakest players in the AI ecosystem — the neoclouds, Oracle, standalone model developers and construction/equipment suppliers — would face acute distress," he added. "The hyperscalers would suffer serious revenue downgrades; and even the promise of lower capital spending (the return of free cash flow) would offer scant consolation. The traditional banking sector would not be immune."
In terms of how this would affect the US economy on a broader level, Perkins said, "A cyclical downturn is inevitable. Capital spending would plunge and confidence evaporate. There would be sizeable job losses in the construction sector. But as far as recessions go, we don't think this one would be particularly severe (at the milder end of historical norms). Not only is the macro footprint of the AI boom smaller than people think, but there is plenty of room for the Fed to cut rates. Ultimately, this policy response would be successful, especially for the bottom of America's K-shaped economy."
The backdrop for tech stocks has become increasingly fraught as October has played out.
Concerns began earlier this month with neocloud company CoreWeave (CRWV).
The company's corporate bonds across maturities continued to be dumped amid fears of an AI slowdown and its implications for the company's precarious balance sheet. That has triggered a subsequent sharp sell-off in the stock.
CoreWeave stock has been crushed in October to the tune of 35%.
Meta (META) then dropped a bombshell in its third quarter results this week, posting negative free cash flow for the first time since 2012 amid aggressive spending on AI.
The company said it would issue a new tranche of stock to help fuel its AI build-out.
Tesla (TSLA) also slashed its capital expenditures plan for the year by $5 billion to $20 billion.

item.title: Oil prices jump $3 on Houthi attacks, oil spill, highest settlement since April
item.author: Nicole Jao
item.description:
Oil prices jump $3 on Houthi attacks, oil spill, highest settlement since April
2026-10-26
Por Nicole Jao
https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/oil-prices-rise-supply-concerns-052617190.html
By Nicole Jao
NEW YORK, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Oil prices settled more than $3 higher on Friday, their highest in nearly six months after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East, where UAE authorities also reported an oil spill.
Brent crude futures settled at $116.72 a barrel, up $3.55 or 3.14%, their highest since April 29. US West Texas Intermediate crude closed at $103.27 a barrel, up $3.80 or 3.8%.
Brent finished the week up 6% and WTI ended 2.3% higher.
"Fears of supply disruptions drove the advance after Iranian-backed Houthi rebels carried out a series of attacks across Saudi Arabia, including on energy infrastructure," said Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist for LPL Financial.
On Thursday, Saudi Aramco ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain, Reuters reported. Fighting intensified between Saudi Arabia, the world's largest crude exporter and Yemen-based Houthis.
An oil spill from a tanker was detected off the UAE coast of Umm Al Quwain, the United Arab Emirates Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said. It did not say what caused the spill and authorities have not identified the tanker involved.
ATTACKS ON VESSELS
Shipping sources said on October 9 that the Gem No. 2 supertanker was struck by an unidentified projectile 13 nautical miles (24 km) west of Al Jazeera in the UAE.
"The market is concerned about these continued Iranian attacks on tankers that we've seen increase over the last week," said Andrew Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. "While there has been an increase in oil transiting out of the Strait of Hormuz, that could change at any minute."
Clashes between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government have raged since the Iran-aligned Houthis pushed towards Bab el-Mandeb Strait last month, a shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea.
October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017.
President Donald Trump said on Friday the US could end the war with Iran quickly, but said perhaps Washington should allow the conflict to gradually wind down.
STRATEGIC RESERVE RELEASES

item.content:encoded:
Oil prices jump $3 on Houthi attacks, oil spill, highest settlement since April

2026-10-26

Por Nicole Jao

https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/oil-prices-rise-supply-concerns-052617190.html

By Nicole Jao

NEW YORK, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Oil prices settled more than $3 higher on Friday, their highest in nearly six months after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East, where UAE authorities also reported an oil spill.

Brent crude futures settled at $116.72 a barrel, up $3.55 or 3.14%, their highest since April 29. US West Texas Intermediate crude closed at $103.27 a barrel, up $3.80 or 3.8%.

Brent finished the week up 6% and WTI ended 2.3% higher.

"Fears of supply disruptions drove the advance after Iranian-backed Houthi rebels carried out a series of attacks across Saudi Arabia, including on energy infrastructure," said Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist for LPL Financial.

On Thursday, Saudi Aramco ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain, Reuters reported. Fighting intensified between Saudi Arabia, the world's largest crude exporter and Yemen-based Houthis.

An oil spill from a tanker was detected off the UAE coast of Umm Al Quwain, the United Arab Emirates Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said. It did not say what caused the spill and authorities have not identified the tanker involved.

ATTACKS ON VESSELS

Shipping sources said on October 9 that the Gem No. 2 supertanker was struck by an unidentified projectile 13 nautical miles (24 km) west of Al Jazeera in the UAE.

"The market is concerned about these continued Iranian attacks on tankers that we've seen increase over the last week," said Andrew Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. "While there has been an increase in oil transiting out of the Strait of Hormuz, that could change at any minute."

Clashes between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government have raged since the Iran-aligned Houthis pushed towards Bab el-Mandeb Strait last month, a shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea.

October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017.

President Donald Trump said on Friday the US could end the war with Iran quickly, but said perhaps Washington should allow the conflict to gradually wind down.

STRATEGIC RESERVE RELEASES

The US Department of Energy said it had authorized an emergency exchange of up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address a supply disruption affecting Phillips 66's Lake Charles refinery in Louisiana.

item.title: Warsh Tells Traders to Watch the Data. They Still Follow the Fed
item.author: Enda Curran; Ye Xie; Victor Swezey
item.description:
Warsh Tells Traders to Watch the Data. They Still Follow the Fed
2026-10-26
Por Enda Curran; Ye Xie; Victor Swezey
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/warsh-tells-traders-watch-data-150000451.html
(Bloomberg) -- Early on Oct. 14, just hours before the release of a much-anticipated report on US inflation, TD Securities' Gennadiy Goldberg recommended that clients bet against a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike later in the month. The logic was that inflation would likely be benign enough to justify a hold. Equally important, a slew of Fed officials had spent days pushing back against expectations for an imminent move.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Then the data came in hot. Traders quickly ramped up bets on an October hike, at one point putting the odds at roughly 50-50, up from about 20% before the report — and Goldberg and his team began debating whether to abandon their brand-new trade. But almost as quickly as the market moved against them, it started swinging back. By the end of the day, most of that move had been erased. "We didn't even have a chance to take the trade off," said Goldberg, head of US interest-rate strategy.
Several market cross-currents were at play that day to stoke the roundtrip, including a stock selloff, AI jitters and increasing tensions in France. For many, though, it came down to the stream of Fedspeak signaling a pause in October. The seemingly explicit language stood out at a time when Chairman Kevin Warsh has said he wants to wean markets off such "forward guidance."
Caught in the middle, traders fell back on the familiar and took their cue from what policymakers were saying. But they also acknowledge that on its own, the inflation data might have spurred them to wager on an October hike. All of this leaves investors in a precarious position heading into this week's policy meeting, still somewhat guessing and prone to a jolt if their read of the situation turns out to be wrong.
"There's a disconnect between what Warsh has said and what the others have signaled," said Neil Dutta, head of economics at Renaissance Macro Research. "When you have this sort of development or condition, there's always a risk that the market can get whipsawed at any given meeting."
To be sure, recent market developments make the chance of such a whipsaw less likely. With AI shares continuing to slide and concerns starting to build around US growth prospects should the artificial intelligence boom falter, traders now have even less conviction that the Fed will raise rates next week — or even this year. Odds of an October move now stand at less than 15%, based on interest-rate swaps. But it was a different picture just a few weeks ago, when the series of speeches began.
The backdrop was a brutal bond selloff that had sent US yields sharply higher. The Fed had raised rates in September for the first time in three years, and expectations were building for an October hike and possibly another in December, all in the name of cooling an inflation rate that has persistently run ahead of the central bank's target.
Tamping the Brakes
This was the vibe when, on Sept. 29, Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams said one more interest-rate hike "late this year" may be appropriate. That speech prompted traders to ratchet back the probability of an October hike slump to about 50% from 70%, based on federal funds futures contracts.
Williams was followed two days later on Oct. 1 by Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, who suggested policymakers should take more time before deciding whether additional hikes are needed, views that sent market bets tumbling further toward 25%. A speech by Governor Christopher Waller on Oct. 8 that said officials don't need to tighten at consecutive meetings was enough to cement the outlook.
"I think they were looking at the bond market and saying, 'Whoa, they're pricing in a lot more aggressive rate hikes than we are expecting,'" said Nationwide Chief Economist Kathy Bostjan
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: Weight-loss drugs fuel protein boom, but with more consumer scrutiny
item.author: Waylon Cunningham; Nicholas P Brown
item.description:
Weight-loss drugs fuel protein boom, but with more consumer scrutiny
2026-10-26
Por Waylon Cunningham; Nicholas P Brown
https://finance.yahoo.com/healthcare/articles/weight-loss-drugs-fuel-protein-091415957.html
Oct 23 (Reuters) - Protein-infused bottled water. Ice cream. Boxed macaroni and cheese. Even vodka.
The rise of weight-loss drugs is driving a boom in protein-based products, as users of GLP-1 medication like Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Eli Lilly's Mounjaro look for ways to counter the muscle loss those drugs can cause. GLP-1 users say they will spend 11% more on high-protein foods than before starting the drugs, according to an August survey from Boston Consulting Group.
Even as consumers seek out new sources of protein for their diets, they are becoming more skeptical of foods advertised as high-protein, Reuters interviews with consumers and company executives found. Some shoppers question whether products contain as much protein as advertising implies, while blanching at those that pack in so many additives or sugar that they undercut the health pitch.
A report from marketing research firm NielsenIQ earlier this year said the snack industry has entered its "accountability era," noting that 25% of its survey respondents this year said they are using scanning apps to check the nutritional value of products, up from around 17% last year.
"Protein is no longer a differentiator," said Chris Costagli, a lead marketing researcher at NielsenIQ, who co-wrote the report.
Megan Gisela Bautista, a nonprofit employee in Maryland who does strength training, was recently disappointed by the protein content of a chicken jerky snack that touted high protein in a large, colorful font.
"I'd have to eat five of them," Bautista said. "That's bad for you."
"As this protein craze pops off, and things are getting more expensive, I want to be sure what I'm putting in my body is healthy," Spears said.
Some brands acknowledge the growing consumer scrutiny.
"Protein is here to stay, but the conversation must evolve," said Susan Zaripheh, North America chief research officer for yogurt maker Danone, in a statement to Reuters. "Consumers are starting to look 'beyond the gram,' becoming more informed in the nuances of protein source and nutrient density."
Over the summer, the French food company filed a false advertising lawsuit against rival yogurt maker Chobani, accusing it of inflating its protein claims on labels by using non-standard serving sizes. Chobani has disputed those claims, telling Reuters in a statement that its labeling is accurate and transparent.
Zaripheh said consumers want products that also aid in digestibility and contain other nutrients like fiber. In addition to existing high-protein yogurts and soy milks, the company is developing products that combine protein with other nutrients.
Globe Market Research estimated over the summer that the worldwide protein-enriched food market was worth nearly $58 billion last year.
But Hormel Foods, well-known for protein-heavy products like Spam and canned lunch meats, said it is avoiding the use of additives to increase protein in its products.
"We believe that in the long run, people don't want too much science in their food," said Jason Levine, Hormel chief marketing officer, referring to additives like "whey powder or pea powder or scientifically engineered protein isolates."
SCRUTINIZING LABELS
Reuters found several brands that advertise protein content based on a larger portion size than used in regular versions of the same product, including in pastas, oatmeals and granolas.
Nature Valley, a snack brand owned by General Mills, sells a version of its "oats 'n honey" loose granola that advertises 13 grams of protein on its packaging, based on a 2/3 cup (65 grams) serving size, more than twice as big as the 1/4 cup (27 grams) it calls a serving size for its regular, non-enhanced granola.
General Mills, in a statement, said it considers the regular version a snack
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: Tesla's flying Roadster is more fuel for SpaceX merger rumors than a real car
item.author: Hamza Shaban
item.description:
Tesla's flying Roadster is more fuel for SpaceX merger rumors than a real car
2026-10-26
Por Hamza Shaban
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/teslas-flying-roadster-is-more-fuel-for-spacex-merger-rumors-than-a-real-car-155008011.html
Tesla, strictly speaking, is a car company. But CEO Elon Musk has gone out of his way to tell investors he doesn't want it to be. The adrenaline-soaked Roadster EV unveiling — packed with aerial acrobatics — was another reminder.
Tesla (TSLA) was showing off its newest, fastest car. But it was also, in the eyes of many analysts, soft-launching a merger with SpaceX, of engineering, audacious flair, and Musk's ambitions.
The reactions from Tesla's sharpest observers underscored what was left unsaid. "So SpaceX buys Tesla this year. That's has become obvious," wrote Gerber Kawasaki's Ross Gerber, a vocal Tesla shareholder and frequent commentator on Musk's business moves.
In, of course, a post on X.
The flashy Roadster unveiling placed an exclamation point on simmering chatter about an impending tie-up. Rumors and commentary have been circulating for months, highlighting the shared technology and partnerships that would make for a sensible marriage. Musk himself has heavily hinted at combining his two biggest companies, including on Tesla's latest earnings call. And last month, at the All-In Summit, he emphasized the collaboration between the two.
In a note to clients earlier this month, Barclays analyst Dan Levy said a tie-up "has increasingly become the consensus expectation." The Roadster event — light on details about the actual car business, but heavy on the pizzazz — prompted several other Tesla watchers to hint at or explicitly get behind that forecast.
A note by JPMorgan analysts led by Rajat Gupta pointed to Tesla glossing over what the Roadster means commercially for Tesla, instead showcasing its deep collaboration with SpaceX. Other reactions were more direct.
Gene Munster of Deepwater Management posted his two big takeaways on X, Thursday night. "1. It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers. 2. Elon can't wait to bring Tesla and SpaceX together."
Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said the event strengthened the case for Musk's rocket company and Tesla to operate as one engineering platform. "We believe there is an 80% chance that Tesla and SpaceX merge by the end of 2027 for a number of strategic AI/data driven reasons," he said in a note on Friday.
Hamza Shaban is a reporter for Yahoo Finance covering markets and the economy. Follow Hamza on X @hshaban.

In, of course, a post on X.

The flashy Roadster unveiling placed an exclamation point on simmering chatter about an impending tie-up. Rumors and commentary have been circulating for months, highlighting the shared technology and partnerships that would make for a sensible marriage. Musk himself has heavily hinted at combining his two biggest companies, including on Tesla's latest earnings call. And last month, at the All-In Summit, he emphasized the collaboration between the two.

In a note to clients earlier this month, Barclays analyst Dan Levy said a tie-up "has increasingly become the consensus expectation." The Roadster event — light on details about the actual car business, but heavy on the pizzazz — prompted several other Tesla watchers to hint at or explicitly get behind that forecast.

A note by JPMorgan analysts led by Rajat Gupta pointed to Tesla glossing over what the Roadster means commercially for Tesla, instead showcasing its deep collaboration with SpaceX. Other reactions were more direct.

Gene Munster of Deepwater Management posted his two big takeaways on X, Thursday night. "1. It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers. 2. Elon can't wait to bring Tesla and SpaceX together."

Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said the event strengthened the case for Musk's rocket company and Tesla to operate as one engineering platform. "We believe there is an 80% chance that Tesla and SpaceX merge by the end of 2027 for a number of strategic AI/data driven reasons," he said in a note on Friday.

Hamza Shaban is a reporter for Yahoo Finance covering markets and the economy. Follow Hamza on X @hshaban.

item.title: Trump Says Decision Time Nears on Iran: Deal or ‘Finish It Off’
item.author: María Paula Mijares Torres; Hadriana Lowenkron
item.description:
Trump Says Decision Time Nears on Iran: Deal or ‘Finish It Off’
2026-10-26
Por María Paula Mijares Torres; Hadriana Lowenkron
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/trump-says-decision-time-nears-145705688.html
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump said it's "getting to be decision time" on whether he will make a deal with Tehran or resume attacks as Iranian and Houthi threats against Americans in the Middle East continue to grow.
Most Read from Bloomberg
"I have a decision to make: Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal? That's all," Trump said in an interview with Fox News' Sunday Morning Futures. "We don't play games."
Trump has suggested that US strikes on Iran could resume after the Nov. 3 midterm elections and he has sent additional forces, including a third aircraft carrier group, toward the Persian Gulf.
Officials warn the period between the election and the new Congress taking office could be particularly dangerous, with a negotiated deal seen as the most likely way to end the conflict.
The US is reducing diplomatic and military staffing in parts of the Middle East amid growing threats from Iran and the Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen.
The State Department had initially acknowledged departures only from Saudi Arabia, but an American official told Bloomberg News Friday that staffing changes are taking place more broadly as Iran intensifies attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz.
Most Read from Bloomberg Businessweek
2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: US consumer sentiment near record low ahead of midterm elections
item.author: Dan Burns
item.description:
US consumer sentiment near record low ahead of midterm elections
2026-10-26
Por Dan Burns
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/us-consumer-sentiment-near-record-141940567.html
By Dan Burns
Oct 23 (Reuters) - US consumer sentiment edged down to near a record low in October as rising prices because of the Middle East conflict soured households' views of the economy on the doorstep of midterm congressional elections centering on affordability issues, a survey showed on Friday.
The University of Michigan's Surveys of Consumers said its Consumer Sentiment Index dropped to 48.0 this month from a final reading of 48.1 in September. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the index at 46.3, which had also been the index's preliminary reading for October.
October's reading marked the second-lowest on record after the all-time low of 44.8 set in May, not long after the Iran war began.
"Purchasing power continues to dominate consumer views of the economy," said Joanne Hsu, the director of the Surveys of Consumers. "Sentiment is now 10% below a year ago and 15% less than February, just prior to the Iran conflict."
The survey results dovetail with political polling data showing voters have a dim view of the economy and President Donald Trump's and the Republican Party's stewardship over it.
Millions of US voters have already cast early ballots in the fast-approaching November 3 midterm election that will determine control of Congress over the final two years of Trump's term. Polls show Republicans are likely to lose control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate as Trump's approval rating in a Reuters/Ipsos poll sits at a record low thanks to the skyrocketing fuel prices unleashed by his decision to attack Iran in late February.
University of Michigan data broken down by political party affiliation showed the weaker sentiment was led by survey respondents self-identified as independents, who comprise a critical bloc of swing voters. Their sentiment score dropped to 42.4 — just above May's record-low 40.6 — from 47.7 in September, while scores for Democrats and Republicans improved.
The survey showed a significant upswing this year among independents — and also notably Republicans — citing high prices as a drag on their personal finances. Since January, the number of independents referencing inflation pressures as hurting their financial situation rose by 27%, while it has shot up by 52% among Republicans. Similar citations among Democrats, meanwhile, are up by 15%.
Households with no or limited exposure to the stock market — until recently climbing rapidly on enthusiasm for the artificial intelligence investment boom — also have cited high prices as a drag on their finances more frequently than at the start of the year.

item.title: Fed expected to hold rates steady this week ahead of midterms, signal they’re not done raising rates
item.author: Jennifer Schonberger
item.description:
Fed expected to hold rates steady this week ahead of midterms, signal they’re not done raising rates
2026-10-26
Por Jennifer Schonberger
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article/fed-expected-to-hold-rates-steady-this-week-despite-hot-inflation--but-signal-theyre-not-done-hiking-210000926.html
Fed expected to hold rates steady this week despite hot inflation — but signal they're not done hiking
The Federal Reserve heads into its interest-rate decision this week facing hotter inflation, keeping the meeting live even as markets widely expect the central bank to hold interest rates steady just days before the midterm elections.
Alan Blinder, a former Fed vice chair and a Princeton University economics professor, is expecting a "hawkish pause."
Although Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh doesn't favor telegraphing the central bank's next move, Blinder said the moment calls for clarity.
"This is a perfect time for clear forward guidance that doesn't quite say, but strongly hints, we're pausing now, but we stand ready to raise again and even give a hint that the next meeting might be the next interest rate hike."
Inflation heated up in September, as the Consumer Price Index accelerated to 3.7% from a year earlier. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, ticked up to 2.6%, while wholesale prices jumped more than 6%, and the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — the core Personal Consumption Expenditures index — is projected to top 3%.
In his last remarks before this week's policy meeting, many observers think Warsh underscored what Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed president John Williams previously said: that despite hot inflation reports, they would like to take time to review the data as they consider the prospect of further rate hikes.
Read more: How jobs, inflation, and the Fed are all related
Warsh neither endorsed nor pushed back on his colleagues' recent signals that they'd like to wait for more data, but he noted that the world had "broadly conformed to our expectations" since the Fed's September meeting.
After raising rates for the first time in more than three years in September, minutes from that meeting read that most participants assessed that another increase would likely be appropriate by year-end.
Ken Rogoff, Harvard University professor and former chief economist of the International Monetary Fund, told Yahoo Finance he thinks the Fed will hold rates steady next week because of the proximity to the midterm elections less than a week later.
"The fundamentals call for raising the rate," Rogoff said. "If you didn't have an election, they should hike … But they are going to hold rates steady and talk about how they're probably going to increase it once or twice at least in the near future."
Blinder agrees that the midterms are part of the consideration. "When it's that close to an election there's something to be said for keeping your head down," he said, noting that while it is far from the only factor, election proximity serves as a "minus" in the mental basket for raising rates.

item.title: Inflation under Trump is only about half the rate under Biden. Voters are still just as mad.
item.author: Ben Werschkul
item.description:
Inflation under Trump is only about half the rate under Biden. Voters are still just as mad.
2026-10-26
Por Ben Werschkul
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article/inflation-under-trump-is-only-about-half-the-rate-under-biden-voters-are-still-just-as-mad-120043933.html
So far in President Trump's second term, prices in the US have risen only about half as quickly as during his predecessor's four years in office. Yet Trump has a 72% disapproval rating on the issue and risks paying a steep political price — just as former President Biden did — with voters drawing a direct connection between rising prices and the president's policies.
During the last election cycle, prices of all items rose more than 20% in Biden's term, sparking widespread voter angst. This time around, price growth is notably slower, rising 5.4% in a little less than the two years since Inauguration Day.
But a Yahoo Finance analysis of price data shows that a few major outliers have hit Americans' wallets disproportionately, largely due to increases in goods affected by the war in Iran and tariffs.
Fuel oil and gasoline are perhaps the most dramatic examples, spiking over 30% beginning in March in response to the war in Iran and the closing of the Strait of Hormuz.
And voters have noticed, as evidenced in poll after poll. A New York Times/Siena poll released this week found 73% of likely voters disapprove of the president's handling of gas prices.
Trump underscored the salience of energy prices when he posted a charge this week that "Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the US Midterm Election."
Trump has often pushed back against questions about high energy prices, saying they won't be a problem once the war in Iran ends.
Read more: How oil price shocks ripple through your wallet, from gas to groceries
Link between price spikes and Trump policies
The connection between price increases and Trump's tariff policy has also been in evidence.
Coffee prices have risen nearly 23% during Trump's second term (more than double the rate under Biden) as tariffs raised prices before Trump scrapped many of the coffee duties late last year in response to coffee drinkers' unhappiness.
Goods like toys and footwear have likewise risen rapidly as importers from China and elsewhere in Asia faced new tariffs. Toys are a particularly stark example, falling by 4.6% during Biden's term and then rising by 7.8% so far in Trump's term.
"Maybe the children will have two dolls instead of 30 dolls, and maybe the two dolls will cost a couple of bucks more than they would normally," Trump said in a rare acknowledgment of tariff-fueled price increases when he was pressed on the issue in April.
Other goods have moved in the opposite direction. Eggs jumped by an average of 2.57% each month when Biden was in the White House, but have dropped 3.82% each month of Trump's term so far, the analysis shows.

But a Yahoo Finance analysis of price data shows that a few major outliers have hit Americans' wallets disproportionately, largely due to increases in goods affected by the war in Iran and tariffs.
Fuel oil and gasoline are perhaps the most dramatic examples, spiking over 30% beginning in March in response to the war in Iran and the closing of the Strait of Hormuz.
And voters have noticed, as evidenced in poll after poll. A New York Times/Siena poll released this week found 73% of likely voters disapprove of the president's handling of gas prices.
Trump underscored the salience of energy prices when he posted a charge this week that "Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the US Midterm Election."
Trump has often pushed back against questions about high energy prices, saying they won't be a problem once the war in Iran ends.
Read more: How oil price shocks ripple through your wallet, from gas to groceries
Link between price spikes and Trump policies
The connection between price increases and Trump's tariff policy has also been in evidence.
Coffee prices have risen nearly 23% during Trump's second term (more than double the rate under Biden) as tariffs raised prices before Trump scrapped many of the coffee duties late last year in response to coffee drinkers' unhappiness.
Goods like toys and footwear have likewise risen rapidly as importers from China and elsewhere in Asia faced new tariffs. Toys are a particularly stark example, falling by 4.6% during Biden's term and then rising by 7.8% so far in Trump's term.
"Maybe the children will have two dolls instead of 30 dolls, and maybe the two dolls will cost a couple of bucks more than they would normally," Trump said in a rare acknowledgment of tariff-fueled price increases when he was pressed on the issue in April.
Other goods have moved in the opposite direction. Eggs jumped by an average of 2.57% each month when Biden was in the White House, but have dropped 3.82% each month of Trump's term so far, the analysis shows.

item.title: Private Fund Valuations, AI Risks to Be Focus of SEC Examiners
item.author: Nicola M White
item.description:
Private Fund Valuations, AI Risks to Be Focus of SEC Examiners
2026-10-26
Por Nicola M White
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/private-fund-valuations-ai-risks-140000139.html
(Bloomberg) -- Securities and Exchange Commission examiners will step up scrutiny of private fund valuations and artificial intelligence, the latest sign of regulatory concerns about emerging market risk.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Investment advisers, brokers, clearing agencies and others can expect staffers at the Wall Street watchdog to focus on fees, expenses and valuations in private funds, according to the agency's Division of Examinations priorities released Friday. The agency also plans to zoom in on how firms prepare for AI-related cyberattacks.
The focus on private fund valuations and credit comes as the SEC considers expanding retail investor access to private markets, including private equity and early-stage startups that have been historically off-limits to the general public.
At the same time, private credit managers have faced a wave of redemption requests as anxious investors try to cash out. Examiners will spend time on what the SEC calls retail investor protection, particularly for complex, higher-risk, and illiquid products, the agency said.
Although artificial intelligence has been listed as a priority for examiners in previous years, the SEC went into further details this year to reflect rapid changes in technology, including cybersecurity.
Examiners will focus on how AI-fueled attacks may affect firms' businesses or customers, such as through phishing messages and deepfake voice and video used for social engineering.
The SEC publishes its examinations priorities every year to signal how it aims to promote compliance, identify fraud, and monitor risks. Exam staffers sometimes escalate findings to the agency's enforcement division for further investigation.
The staff also examines so-called self-regulatory organizations, such as the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, the regulator for broker-dealers.
"Examinations are one of the Commission's most important tools for promoting compliance with the federal securities laws and helping protect investors," SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins said in a statement.
This year, the examinations staff added the US audit regulator, the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board, to its list of examination targets. Queries could include whether the board, which regulates auditors, would include whether the organization is is following its own policies and procedures.

item.title: OpenAI aiming for new $30 billion funding round at a $1.25 trillion valuation
item.author: Daniel Howley
item.description:
OpenAI aiming for new $30 billion funding round at a $1.25 trillion valuation
2026-10-25
Por Daniel Howley
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/openai-aiming-for-new-30-billion-funding-round-at-a-125-trillion-valuation-131325168.html
OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) is looking to raise a fresh $30 billion funding round that would value the AI lab at $1.25 trillion. The company was previously looking to raise capital at a $1.5 trillion valuation, according to Bloomberg.
OpenAI last raised $122 billion in March, which valued the company at $852 billion.
Rival Anthropic (ANTH.PVT), meanwhile, is preparing to file its initial public offering (IPO) ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, with Wall Street anticipating a valuation of as high as $2 trillion.
The company could publicly reveal its S-1 at any time in the coming days.
OpenAI's funding discussions come amid wide-ranging declines in AI stocks on Wall Street over concerns about the data center build-out. Neoclouds, especially CoreWeave (CRWV), have been at the center of the latest rout, with investors questioning the companies' enormous debt loads.
Everything from semiconductor to hyperscaler stocks has taken a hit, with Meta (META) dropping as much as 7% on Thursday after raising the lower end of its capital expenditure guidance.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (^SOX) is off 7% in the past 5 days.

item.title: Brent crude tops $116 as traders price escalating Middle East conflict
item.author: Ines Ferré
item.description:
Brent crude tops $116 as traders price escalating Middle East conflict
2026-10-25
Por Ines Ferré
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/brent-crude-tops-116-as-traders-price-in-middle-east-escalation-192101547.html
Oil prices climbed to a 6-month high on Friday as traders priced the odds of escalating fighting in the Middle East. Attacks near the Red Sea also stoked worries of further constraints on oil supplies from the region.
Brent crude (BZ=F) futures for December delivery settled at $116.72 per barrel. The international benchmark posted its third consecutive week of gains. Meanwhile, West Texas Intermediate crude (CL=F) closed just above $103 a barrel.
President Trump telegraphed an escalation in Iran after the midterm elections and an extended stand-off, with the Strait of Hormuz remaining at the center of the conflict.
This week, the New York Times reported that the US and Israel have reportedly drawn up plans for renewed attacks on Iran after the Nov. 3 elections. The US has ordered nonessential embassy personnel to depart Saudi Arabia after a series of attacks at the country's airports and oil fields.
President Trump has said he will not attack Iran before the midterms and has suggested that fuel prices will fall afterward.
Meanwhile, the Red Sea area has seen increased attacks recently, including on Saudi Arabian airports and on an Aramco oil field this week.
Saudi Aramco on Thursday ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran, marking the oil giant's first such evacuation since the Iran war began.
On Friday, the national price of gasoline stood at $4.29 per gallon, roughly $1.22 higher than a year ago. Diesel hovered around $6.31, about $2.68 more than this time last year.
A power outage at a refinery in the Chicago area is expected to send refined fuel prices even higher in the region.
"You're going to see a lot of $5 gas prices in places like Michigan, Ohio, Minnesota, Illinois, and Indiana," Gulf Oil chief energy adviser Tom Kloza told Yahoo Finance on Thursday.
Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

item.title: SK Hynix pulls a $150 billion IPO as its own record US listing sits underwater
item.author: Jared Blikre
item.description:
SK Hynix pulls a $150 billion IPO as its own record US listing sits underwater
2026-10-25
Por Jared Blikre
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/sk-hynix-pulls-a-150-billion-ipo-as-its-own-record-us-listing-sits-underwater-134006966.html
In July, SK Hynix (SKHY) raised $26.5 billion in the biggest US listing ever by a foreign company. Now the company is walking away from one of the biggest tech IPOs ever.
The South Korean memory giant said Friday it has shelved plans to list Solidigm, its flash memory unit, in the US, citing market conditions and share price trends. Solidigm had aimed to raise $10 billion to $15 billion at a valuation of up to $150 billion, according to industry estimates cited by the Wall Street Journal.
For a clue to why, look at the company's own stock.
SK Hynix priced its US shares at $149 in July. SK Hynix stock is rising on Friday but still trades below that price, about a third below the stock's September record.
SK Hynix has plenty of company
Memory and storage stocks have shed $1.3 trillion in market value from their 2026 records, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. SK Hynix accounts for about $489 billion of that, and Micron (MU) accounts for about $411 billion. Of the 59 chip stocks in a Yahoo Finance basket, 58 are down in October.
That's a strange look for an industry printing money. Memory makers are booking record profits on AI data center demand, and executives see shortages lasting into 2028. The stocks are trading as if the peak is already in, after a $3 trillion chip rout this month.
Solidigm isn't the only AI-linked deal getting pulled back. Australian data center operator Firmus Grid canceled its IPO, and AirTrunk delayed its Singapore listing to next year. OpenAI is now seeking a $1.25 trillion valuation in funding talks, down from $1.4 trillion. Anthropic's (ANTH.PVT) blockbuster IPO is expected next month.
The next test for memory stocks comes on Thursday, when Sandisk (SNDK) reports after the close.
For SK Hynix, watch $149. A move back above its IPO price would put July's buyers back in the black. Until then, it's a ceiling.

item.title: Trump ends tariffs on some Canadian products, as Senator Collins faces close race
item.author: David Shepardson
item.description:
Trump ends tariffs on some Canadian products, as Senator Collins faces close race
2026-10-25
Por David Shepardson
https://finance.yahoo.com/news/us-expected-remove-50-tariffs-180534074.html
By David Shepardson
WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - With an incumbent Maine US senator from his own party locked in a tight reelection battle, President Donald Trump signed an order on Friday to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products in a move that could benefit companies from the northern state.
The Republican president's hefty tariffs on Canada have caused friction with the US neighbor to the north while creating problems for American businesses in Maine and other states that rely on certain Canadian goods.
With the November 3 US midterm elections looming and Republicans fighting to retain control of both houses of Congress, Senator Susan Collins had urged the White House to address tariffs on products affecting companies and farmers in Maine, a state that borders Canada.
COLLINS, IN TIGHT MAINE RACE, PRAISES TARIFF RELIEF
Trump's order exempted plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and packing crates and boxes, as well as fresh and dried seaweed, the White House said.
The changes take effect on October 30, four days before the election.
Trump added a number of Canadian products to the 50% tariff list to offset the tariff relief provided in his order, including carpets, paints, waste, shampoos, cocoa powder, wooden coffins, ice cream sticks, air-conditioning machines, chest freezers, archery equipment and canoes.
Collins said the relief would aid Maine's blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers.
"These producers are a vital part of our state's economy and support our rural and coastal communities," Collins said. "Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense."
Democrat Troy Jackson is seeking to oust Collins in a race that polls indicate is very close. The two sparred over tariffs at an October 6 debate.
"Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers," Jackson said on Friday after Trump's action. "Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire."
Collins did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Jackson's remarks.
Trump in August imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian imports, which took effect after talks between the two countries collapsed. Canada retaliated in September with tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on $20 billion in US goods.

item.itunes:summary:
Trump ends tariffs on some Canadian products, as Senator Collins faces close race
2026-10-25
Por David Shepardson
https://finance.yahoo.com/news/us-expected-remove-50-tariffs-180534074.html
By David Shepardson
WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - With an incumbent Maine US senator from his own party locked in a tight reelection battle, President Donald Trump signed an order on Friday to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products in a move that could benefit companies from the northern state.
The Republican president's hefty tariffs on Canada have caused friction with the US neighbor to the north while creating problems for American businesses in Maine and other states that rely on certain Canadian goods.
With the November 3 US midterm elections looming and Republicans fighting to retain control of both houses of Congress, Senator Susan Collins had urged the White House to address tariffs on products affecting companies and farmers in Maine, a state that borders Canada.
COLLINS, IN TIGHT MAINE RACE, PRAISES TARIFF RELIEF
Trump's order exempted plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and packing crates and boxes, as well as fresh and dried seaweed, the White House said.
The changes take effect on October 30, four days before the election.
Trump added a number of Canadian products to the 50% tariff list to offset the tariff relief provided in his order, including carpets, paints, waste, shampoos, cocoa powder, wooden coffins, ice cream sticks, air-conditioning machines, chest freezers, archery equipment and canoes.
Collins said the relief would aid Maine's blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers.
"These producers are a vital part of our state's economy and support our rural and coastal communities," Collins said. "Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense."
Democrat Troy Jackson is seeking to oust Collins in a race that polls indicate is very close. The two sparred over tariffs at an October 6 debate.
"Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers," Jackson said on Friday after Trump's action. "Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire."
Collins did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Jackson's remarks.
Trump in August imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian imports, which took effect after talks between the two countries collapsed. Canada retaliated in September with tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on $20 billion in US goods.

item.title: Wall Street’s safest stock is having its biggest day since the pandemic crash — here’s why investors are paying up
item.author: Jared Blikre
item.description:
Wall Street’s safest stock is having its biggest day since the pandemic crash — here’s why investors are paying up
2026-10-25
Por Jared Blikre
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/wall-streets-safest-stock-just-had-its-biggest-day-since-the-pandemic-crash-chart-of-the-day-100000879.html
Investors are paying tech stock prices for detergent and diapers.
Procter & Gamble (PG), the maker of Tide, Pampers, and Charmin, had its best day since March 2020 on Thursday, adding more than $20 billion in market value. The stock closed at its highest level since February, just shy of its 2026 high, even as the broader market slid.
P&G gave investors exactly what they wanted: steady growth. Sales rose 4% in its fiscal first quarter, mostly because people bought more of its products. The unit that makes Tide and P&G's other cleaning products grew 5%. The company also stuck with its full-year outlook.
"The consumer is with us," CFO Andre Schulten told Yahoo Finance on Thursday. In a market searching for safety, that was enough.
Investors are paying up for safety
P&G now costs more than some of the biggest names in tech.
Investors often gauge how expensive a stock is using the price-to-earnings ratio (P/E), which divides the stock price by the company's earnings per share. Using next year's expected earnings, P&G trades at about 22 times. That's more than Microsoft (MSFT), Meta (META), and Nvidia (NVDA), which trade at less than two-thirds of P&G's multiple.
Tech stocks have been getting cheaper because Wall Street is penciling in stronger future earnings, which makes the "E" in P/E get bigger and the ratio smaller. The recent tech sell-off has knocked down their stock prices, also lowering valuations.
P&G investors are paying a hefty price for a company expecting earnings growth of 3% at most this year.
So why pay up? Investors are paying for predictability. People keep buying toothpaste and toilet paper no matter what the economy does, so P&G's earnings rarely surprise to the downside. When markets get rocky, that kind of reliability becomes more valuable.
The whole aisle is rallying
P&G isn't alone. Kimberly-Clark (KMB), the maker of Kleenex and Huggies, and Colgate-Palmolive (CL) each gained 4% to 5% on Thursday, and Coca-Cola (KO) closed at a record.
The Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLP), which holds the household names people shop for every week, just had its best 13-day run since April 2020. Thursday alone was its best day since April 2025. Over the same stretch, the S&P 500 (^GSPC) has slipped and chip stocks have taken a beating.
Falling interest rates are also helping. Staples stocks are often treated like bonds because they pay steady dividends. When Treasury yields fall, as they did sharply on Thursday, those dividends look more attractive by comparison.

item.title: Amex to Cut 5% of Headcount Globally as Cost Pressures Mount
item.author: Paige Smith; Romaine Bostick
item.description:
Amex to Cut 5% of Headcount Globally as Cost Pressures Mount
2026-10-25
Por Paige Smith; Romaine Bostick
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/amex-cut-5-headcount-globally-135235293.html
(Bloomberg) -- American Express Co. is cutting 5% of its headcount globally as Chief Executive Officer Steve Squeri seeks to keep a lid on the company's rising costs.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Squeri told Bloomberg TV that the company has 78,000 employees, meaning the move will affect about 3,500 jobs.
Financial firms have been cutting jobs in recent months, with some companies attributing the changes to the increased use of artificial intelligence. This week, Barclays Plc said it would eliminate 5,000 jobs. HSBC Holdings Plc is planning job reductions across its UK wealth-management business, Bloomberg News reported earlier this month, and Citigroup Inc. has also been lowering its headcount.
Squeri said on a call with analysts Friday that the job cuts reflect the desire to make the company more agile and efficient, and find ways to reduce layers and speed up decision making.
The company has also been facing consistent pressure to keep and retain its premium card members. To do that, Amex has been refreshing certain cards, adding a raft of new perks last year to its Platinum card. Earlier this month, the company said it would work with Airbnb Inc. to allow for certain luxury rentals on its travel site to count for the cardholders' annual lodging credit.
Overall, that's boosted costs. The New York-based firm said expenses climbed about 9% to $14.5 billion in the third quarter, although it was less than the $14.8 billion estimate from analysts.
Costs for member rewards were up 10% in the quarter, while marketing expenses rose 11%. Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec had previously said to expect marketing expenses to increase by around 10% in the second half of 2026 compared with last year.
"It's been highly competitive," Squeri said about the fight for premium cardholders on the call. "And our assumption is that it will remain highly competitive."
Amex shares were down 1.8% to $319.45 at 9:35 a.m. in New York trading Friday, extending this year's drop to nearly 14%.
Card Spending
The workforce cuts were announced after Amex posted third-quarter earnings that beat estimates, with adjusted earnings per share of $4.68 surpassing the $4.49 average analyst estimate in a Bloomberg survey.

item.title: SpaceX reportedly wants to lease space on 80,000 cell towers in a bid to challenge Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
SpaceX reportedly wants to lease space on 80,000 cell towers in a bid to challenge Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile
2026-10-25
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/spacex-reportedly-wants-to-lease-space-on-80000-cell-towers-in-a-bid-to-challenge-verizon-att-and-t-mobile-145031793.html
SpaceX reportedly wants to lease space on 80,000 cell towers in a bid to challenge Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile
Elon Musk's SpaceX (SPCX) may be close to sending another message to the telecom giants: We are seriously coming for you.
The company is looking to lease space on 80,000 cell sites across the US, Bloomberg reported on Thursday. SpaceX is reportedly in talks with two of the largest owners of cellular towers, Crown Castle and American Tower.
"Committing ~$30 billion into spectrum is serious enough. Committing to 80K macro sites could be a point of no return," Bernstein analyst Laurent Yoon said. "That is a meaningful number, broadly consistent with the scale required for a nationwide terrestrial wireless network. Whether SpaceX ultimately leases anything close to that figure remains uncertain, but the reported scope suggests a far greater level of commitment than spectrum accumulation alone."
AT&T (T), Verizon (VZ), and T-Mobile (TMUS) stock were sharply lower in morning trading.
Earlier this month, SpaceX said it acquired a nationwide low-band spectrum portfolio.
Concerns had already escalated across Wall Street that Starlink could disrupt legacy wireless operators like AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile by transitioning from a rural broadband service into a direct mobile competitor.
Following its strategic acquisition of terrestrial spectrum and rapid deployment of advanced satellites, SpaceX had laid the groundwork to launch its own standalone cellular network alongside its direct-to-cell capabilities.
"Starlink broadband is the threat investors can see today and one that incumbents are beginning to acknowledge," Yoon said. "Starlink Mobile remains the larger long-term question given the size and profitability of the wireless market. The competitive impact may still be years away, but anticipation alone, reinforced by each successive spectrum and infrastructure move, is likely to remain an overhang on sector sentiment."

item.title: There's No Off Switch for Digital Parenting
item.author: Newsletter
item.description:
There's No Off Switch for Digital Parenting
2026-10-25
Por Newsletter
The quiet, often exhausting work of keeping up with kids' digital lives, and how to share it.
The Parent Edit
By Jill Murphy, Common Sense Media
Edition #35 | October 23, 2026
The Second Shift That Is Digital Parenting
Feel free to read this part aloud to your partner, co-parent, or any other supporting caregiver in your family's life. ;) Seriously. As if the usual responsibilities of being an adult
and
a parent aren't enough, digital parenting comes with its own running list: Parental controls. Decisions. Updates. Dashboards. Finding the good apps. Blocking the bad content. Keeping up with the workarounds. Plus the quiet dread of constantly wondering whether you've missed something.
And that's just the devices.
This is why I'm always telling parents, "Give me a scary movie any day." A scary movie has been scripted, edited, and produced by professionals. I know what's in it. I can read a review. It's everything I
can't
preview that worries me: the posts, the comments, the texts, the things my kids come across when I'm not there, and whether those things are lodging somewhere in their mind. Sometimes I wonder what they've seen that they were too scared, too embarrassed, or simply too used to seeing to think they should tell me about it.
The Digital Mental Load is all too real.
If you're sharing the parenting, you should be sharing this part, too.
Learn the platforms. You don't need to know every feature. But know how your kids are using them, where the settings live, and enough to follow the conversation when something comes up.
Take the lead on some of the hard stuff. Own part of the setup, the monitoring, or the "no, not that app" conversations, so the person who usually handles it gets to enjoy some of the fun. We want to pick the movie and share the funny videos with the kids too!
Share the parental controls. Running this space can feel like a second job. If one person always knows the passwords, settings, rules, and latest workaround, that person is probably carrying too much of it. Split up what you can.
Tonight's to-do:
Think about one part of the digital load you could hand off, share, or ask another caregiver to take on this month. Here are some
tips for setting tech boundaries with your children's caregivers
Maybe your toddler is stuck on a loop of one show. Maybe your 7-year-old is suddenly watching a teen creator aimed at much older kids. Whatever the reason, Netflix
does
let you block specific titles. The annoying part: You have to do it one by one.
The fix, for now: Block specific shows
Go to
Account
, then
Profiles
, and choose your child's profile.
Open
Viewing restrictions
. Netflix will ask for your account password.
Under
Title restrictions
, type each show's name, and select it to block it.
Save.
The blocked shows disappear from that profile, though it can take a little while to update on the TV.
A few other tips to help for now:
Lower the maturity rating.
Some creator shows aimed at older kids may disappear automatically if the profile is set to a younger rating.
Lock the other profiles.
Add a PIN to adult profiles so kids can't easily switch over.
Check back occasionally.
Netflix is adding more creator content, so a title-by-title block list may need updating.
Why "for now"? Because this is a manual, title-by-title fix for what's clearly a growing strategy. Every new creator deal means another name to add. It works, but it puts the work on us.
Tonight's to-do:
Open your kid's Netflix profile in a browser and scroll the kids' row with fresh eyes. If there's something you don't want, block it while you're there. Then check out the
best kids' shows on Netflix.
One More Thing
Thank you for your support, and for receiving what honestly felt like a complete and total disaster with so much kindness. My daughter has been really receptive to what I'm calling her "makeunder." We've been talking a
[Transcripcion recortada]
